note: Acharakkovai 10 makes bathing the removal of impurity on ten occasions; Sivavakkiyar addresses those who bathe daily and whose dirt never goes, asking where the dirt really lies.
teaches: The Siddhar denies the premise the bathing list rests on, that the impurity is where water can reach, whereas the Kural only ranks it below inner purity.

note: Kural 1191 calls the love of those loved back the seedless fruit; Thirikadugam counts embracing women who do not desire one among roads to suffering.
teaches: The akam couplet praises mutual desire from inside love; the ethics verse states the reverse as a rule of conduct, so the need for mutual desire is affirmed in both kinds of poetry.
list_adds: It moves the claim from a lover's lament into counsel, and likens union without desire to entering water at an unused ford.

note: Kural 882 says to fear the enemy who seems like kin; Thirikadugam counts taking by the hand a man formerly enraged against one as the conduct of one about to die.
teaches: The couplet warns against the hidden foe in general; the verse names the concrete act, taking back a former enemy, and states its outcome as death.
list_adds: It puts this misplaced trust beside living in sight of foes and walking unarmed among cattle, all three plain exposures to known danger.

note: Kural 146 says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave one who enters another's home; Thirikadugam puts the man at another's door by night between one who runs at a killing elephant and one who plays with a cobra.
teaches: The couplet lists the moral consequences; the verse's company of items makes the danger bodily and immediate, like courting an elephant or a snake.
list_adds: It frames adultery as reckless risk to life by placing it among two plain acts of physical folly.

note: Kural 719 says those who speak well in a good assembly should not speak in a mean one, even by slip; Pazhamozhi 15 calls fine speech among the unlearned the worst thing for a man and a lapse of conduct.
teaches: Pazhamozhi moves the Kural's rule of assembly into the field of ozhukkam, so speaking to the wrong audience is a fault of character that lowers the speaker, not only a tactical error.
list_adds: it ranks the act as the worst of things for a man and proves it with the conduct maxim, which the couplet does not invoke.

note: Kural 544 says the world embraces the feet of the king who embraces his people; Thirikadugam names such a king as hard to find anywhere.
teaches: The couplet states the reward of the caring king as if it were the order of things; the verse adds that such kings are rare, so the world's embrace is seldom earned.
list_adds: It sets the good king beside a well-conducted youth and a flawless ascetic, three rarities each at odds with his station.

note: The two verses open with the same line on the unlearned man's fine point; 12 has it falter when spoken, 13 has it count for nothing when unspoken.
teaches: Read together they form a dilemma: speaking exposes the unlearned man's insight and silence erases it, so without learning there is no way for it to count.

note: Kural 81 says all household life exists for caring for guests and doing வேளாண்மை; Thirikadugam defines the வேளாளன் as one who does not eat while a guest waits.
teaches: Both books use the vel- word for help to guests; the verse makes it a definition of a person, showing that in this group the name is earned by hospitality, not given by birth or land.
list_adds: It sets the vellalan beside the debt-free man and the grateful man as three kinds of kin worth having.

note: Acharakkovai 3 lists sacrifice among four acts to be guarded and kept fruitful; Kural 259 rates abstaining from killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices.
teaches: The ritual code keeps sacrifice as a thing of value needing protection by conduct, while the Kural prices it below a single act of non-killing, so the two books weigh the same rite very differently.
list_adds: It groups sacrifice with fees, penance and learning as goods that conduct preserves, where the Kural sets sacrifice against non-killing and ranks it lower.

note: Both verses bar the sight of புலை, verse 6 to one in எச்சில், verse 13 to one who has oiled the body.
teaches: The bar on seeing புலை recurs under two different ritual states, which shows it is a standing rule of the code rather than a feature of one kind of impurity.

note: Kural 439 says never admire oneself; Thirikadugam names lineage, learning and victory as things that need not speak of themselves.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule; the verse gives a reason for it in the three strongest cases of worth, each of which has its own witness (an assembly, a king), so self-praise is not only wrong but redundant.
list_adds: It picks the three things most tempting to boast of and attaches to each the audience that proclaims it.

note: Verse 7 defines the four kinds of எச்சில்; verse 8 says what they bar and what keeping them yields.
teaches: The pair shows the book's method: a definition followed by its prohibitions and a reward in learning, so purity rules are presented as a discipline of the scholar.

note: Kural 90 says the guest withers at the host's changed face; Thirikadugam counts arriving worn as a guest in a strange town as a road to suffering.
teaches: The Kural measures hospitality by the host's face; the verse looks from the guest's side and counts dependence on strangers as itself a hardship, which is why the host's face matters so much.
list_adds: It sets guesthood beside an unused ford and an unwilling woman, three ventures whose danger lies in the unknown other side.

note: Naladiyar 312 has the bad scholar, worsted in assembly, slap his shoulders and rise to fight; Pazhamozhi 16 has the unlearned provoke the learned and rise itching for a contest.
teaches: The Naladiyar shows the fight as what follows defeat, Pazhamozhi as what the unlearned man starts; together they mark aggression as the unlearned man's response to learning before and after the contest.
list_adds: its proverb judges the challenge hopeless from the start, while the quatrain warns the disciplined to keep away.

note: Acharakkovai 8 bars recitation while in எச்சில்; Sivavakkiyar says the mantra one recites is itself the mouth's எச்சில்.
teaches: One text guards recitation from impurity and the other calls recitation impure in itself, so the rule that protects the mantra is the Siddhar's evidence that purity of the mouth is a fiction.

note: Kural 773 makes ஊராண்மை the cutting edge of valour, help to a foe in distress; Thirikadugam defines ஊராண்மை by modesty under honour, patience under scorn and unreturned dharma.
teaches: The pair shows one word moving from the battlefield, where it is mercy to the fallen enemy, into everyday conduct, where it is a pride made of self-effacement.
list_adds: It breaks the Kural's single heroic act into three civil ones and calls their sum a pride.

note: Kural 134 says a brahmin can relearn the Veda but is ruined if his conduct declines; Thirikadugam asks every gentle person not to let his character decline, and lists following the Veda-knowers as a separate item.
teaches: The pair shows the same verb குன்று applied to conduct in both, but the Kural ranks conduct above Vedic learning inside one birth, while the Thirikadugam keeps them as two equal items for everyone.
list_adds: It moves the rule of undeclining conduct from the brahmin to all gentle people and places Vedic guidance beside it, not above it.

note: Kural 298 says water gives only outer purity and inner purity is seen through truth; Acharakkovai 10 lists ten occasions when water must remove impurity.
teaches: The Kural concedes the outer purity that the Acharakkovai regulates but makes it the lesser half, so the ten baths answer a question the Kural treats as minor; they are different things, not a contradiction.
list_adds: It turns the Kural's single clause on outer purity into an exact list of the occasions that call for a bath, among them dream, hair-cutting and contact with low people.

note: Kural 794 says a friend of good family who shrinks from blame is worth buying; Thirikadugam makes lasting company with the worthy of an old family a medicine.
teaches: Read together, the couplet gives the price of such company and the verse its use: one pays for it because it cures.
list_adds: It makes the old family's worthy one of three remedies with a chaste wife and a learned friend, so lineage-company is ranked with marriage as a cure.

note: Both poems bring in the dark-handed smith (கருங்கைக் கொல்லன்): in 170 the anvil that takes his hammer is the chief facing his foes; in 180 the poor chief asks his town's smith to forge a spear to feed the bards.
teaches: The smith's forge stands in both poems for the link between fighting and giving: 170 makes the chief the anvil that wears out his enemies, and 180 shows the spear made there as the source of the bards' meal.

note: Acharakkovai 16 makes the teacher one of five elders to be worshipped as gods; Purananuru 183 says learning is worth serving and paying the teacher, and that learning outweighs both seniority and the order of birth.
teaches: Puram 183 gives the reason for the teacher's place and also cuts against the list: the elder brother the Acharakkovai reveres yields to the wiser younger, and a learned man of the lowest order draws the highest to him.

note: Kural 1134 has love's flood sweep away the raft of shame and manliness; Thirikadugam has three men let go of the raft of learning.
teaches: Both use the raft against a flood, but the Kural's raft is carried off by force while the Thirikadugam's is let go by choice, which makes the ethics verse a charge of fault, not a lament.
list_adds: It shows one raft dropped at three stages of life (old age, marriage, renunciation), not one lover's moment.

note: Kural 403 calls the unlearned very good if they keep silent before the learned; Pazhamozhi 13 says silence leaves their insight unshown and so gives no ground for thinking themselves good.
teaches: The Kural's ironic praise of the silent unlearned is limited by Pazhamozhi: silence spares them shame but cannot make them one of the good.
list_adds: its proverb makes silence a nullity, so the goodness the couplet grants the silent unlearned is goodness with nothing in it.

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a benefit received; Thirikadugam defines the man of principle as one who does not forget.
teaches: The couplet condemns ingratitude as unforgivable; the verse turns gratitude into a mark by which one chooses kin, making it a reason to bind oneself to a person.
list_adds: It makes gratitude a qualification for kinship, alongside freedom from debt and hospitality.

note: Both use the god who measured the world with his foot: the invocation worships the stride; the Kural makes all it spanned the reward of a king without sloth.
teaches: The same Trivikrama stride serves the ethics group both as an object of worship and as a measure of worldly gain, so the mythic foot carries devotion in one book and royal ambition in the other.
list_adds: It sets the stride beside two other kicks of the same feet, so the measuring becomes one of three acts that together are the feet worshipped.

note: Kazhuvul's Kaamur is a place of blessed vengai fragrance in 365 and the town thrown into turmoil by the fourteen Velir in 135.
teaches: The same chieftain's town gives one poet the image of calm sweetness for the wife's hair and another the image of a besieged, shaken heart, showing that a puram name entered akam with its whole history, peace and siege alike, available for comparison.

note: 216 says the friend, known by hearing alone and never met for many years, will come; Kural 785 says neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed, feeling alone gives the claim (கிழமை) of friendship.
teaches: The Kural's rule and the king's wager share the technical word கிழமை, so the couplet's claim that friendship needs no meeting has a famous royal case behind it, one staked on a seat kept for a man never seen.

note: Kural 603 says the family of the slothful fool perishes before him; Thirikadugam counts falling into sloth while one's dependants go hungry as painful to all.
teaches: The couplet gives the end of sloth, the family's death; the verse gives its moment, idling while those bound to one hunger, so the harm is seen as it begins.
list_adds: It sets this sloth beside dependence on others and being scorned as unlearned, three humiliations of a man who fails his station.

note: Naladiyar 92 sets death, old age and disease before the reader and tells him to share before eating; Thirikadugam names old age, separation and disease as things to fear more than thieves.
teaches: The quatrain moves from the threats to a remedy (give now), while the verse stops at the threat and calls it theft, so the pair shows a list that diagnoses beside a quatrain that prescribes.
list_adds: It adds the separation of the joined to old age and disease, putting an akam grief among the bodily dreads.

note: Verse 1 makes a wife chaste as Arundhati a medicine; verse 16 makes the man who won a chaste wife deathless.
teaches: Within the book the chaste wife is given two predicates, cure and deathlessness, so she is valued both for what she does for the husband now and for the name she leaves him.

note: Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji calling her words a child's babble he graciously hears; 352 measures the friend's sweetness against a famous bard's new tune for Anji's praise.
teaches: The praise songs for Anji, which Avvai offers modestly as babble, had become in akam a byword for sweetness, showing that puram performances were known to the love poets' audience as celebrated pieces of music.

note: Kural 322 makes sharing food the chief of all precepts; Thirikadugam counts living beside those who do not share their food as something that yields no good.
teaches: The couplet praises the sharer; the verse shows the cost of the non-sharer falling on his neighbours, so sharing is a public good of a settlement, not only a private virtue.
list_adds: It sets the stingy neighbour beside a town without teachers and an assembly without elders, three lacks that make a place barren.

note: Purananuru 18 tells a Pandya that those who join water to land give bodies and life; Thirikadugam says one who digs a drinking well without stint gains an undying body.
teaches: The puram poem credits the builder of water works with the lives of his people; the ethics verse credits the well-digger with his own undying body, so the same act of providing water is rewarded outward in one and inward in the other.

note: Kural 720 likens holding forth before those not of one's own group to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Pazhamozhi 14 says learned speech before the unlearned turns good to bad, as a city is a forest to one without kin.
teaches: Both measure an audience by kinship (தங்கணத்தார், தமர்), but the Kural's nectar is only wasted while Pazhamozhi's good words become harmful, which makes the wrong audience an active danger.
list_adds: its proverb casts the speaker, not the speech, as the one stranded, a man among strangers in a city.

note: Naladiyar 270 says those with understanding are as the learned though they have not studied; Pazhamozhi 11 says one who has neither studied nor listened does not understand clearly and is right only by chance. The conflict holds on the reading that 270's உணர்வுடையார் need no study or hearing at all.
teaches: The pair splits on whether native understanding can stand in for learning: the Naladiyar lets inner sense make a man learned, Pazhamozhi treats an untaught man's right judgement as a windfall.
list_adds: its proverb turns the untaught man's success into chance, the very case the quatrain credits to inner understanding.

note: Kural 233 says only lofty fame stands undying; Thirikadugam names fame as one of three ways to an undying body, with a chaste wife and a public well.
teaches: The couplet makes fame the only deathless thing; the verse widens the routes to it, counting a marriage and a work of public water as equally lasting.
list_adds: It turns the Kural's single route to deathlessness into three, two of them not fame-seeking acts at all.

note: Kural 813 says friends who weigh their gains are no better than thieves; Thirikadugam counts the one who clings by fortune and watches for profit as not to be befriended.
teaches: The Kural shames the calculating friend by comparison; the verse adds when he shows himself, at the turn of fortune, which is also when the liar and the hollow man show themselves.
list_adds: It groups the calculating friend with the liar and the one who claims equality in one's fall, three who fail at reversal.

note: Kural 417 says men of deep heard learning do not speak folly even when mistaken; Thirikadugam says friendship with such men clears the tangle of words.
teaches: The couplet says kelvi keeps its owner's own speech clear; the verse adds that it clears others' confusion, so the virtue passes to the friend.
list_adds: It turns a trait of the learned into a benefit for those who befriend them, and sets it among remedies.

note: Kural 133 says conduct is noble birth and its lapse is low birth; Acharakkovai 2 makes good birth one of eight rewards that unfailing conduct earns.
teaches: Both tie birth to conduct, but the Kural collapses birth into present conduct while the Acharakkovai keeps birth as a real rank that conduct earns, so the same link can dissolve or confirm hierarchy.
list_adds: It sets birth among worldly rewards such as wealth, land and health, so birth becomes a prize of conduct rather than its definition.

note: Kural 451 says the small take small company as kin; Thirikadugam names living as kin of the unlearned as a ruin that comes from ignorance.
teaches: The couplet explains who seeks low company (the small); the verse names why (ignorance) and what follows (ruin), giving the act a cause and a result.
list_adds: It sets low company beside wife-beating and entering a house with petty men, so all three are failures of a householder's judgment.

note: Kural 942 regulates the meal by digestion, eating only after the last meal is spent; Acharakkovai 20 regulates it by direction, posture, silence and worship.
teaches: The two books divide the same act between body and rite: the Kural cares when and how much one eats, the Acharakkovai how one sits and where one looks, and neither addresses the other's concern.
list_adds: It makes the meal a sequence of bodily disciplines, facing east, stillness, silence and worship, none of which concerns the food itself.

note: Kural 414 offers listening as the help left to one who has not studied; Pazhamozhi 11 names study and listening as the two routes and condemns the man who has taken neither.
teaches: Together they show listening as the fallback the Kural concedes and Pazhamozhi makes the minimum, so the man without even that has only luck left.
list_adds: it sets study and hearing side by side as two routes and adds a proverb that strips credit from any lucky hit.

note: Both say the unlearned man's standing falters (சோர்வு படும்) when he speaks; Pazhamozhi 12 places it before the learned and gives the cause through its proverb.
teaches: The Kural states the faltering bare and leaves the hearer unnamed; Pazhamozhi supplies the learned hearers and the mechanism, the questions every claim must meet.
list_adds: the proverb explains why the speech falters: among the learned every statement must survive a question it has never faced.

note: Kural 127 says whatever else one fails to guard, guard the tongue; Thirikadugam singles out the unguarded talk of a man who is not drunk.
teaches: Adding 'not drunk' removes the one excuse for loose speech, so the verse sharpens the couplet: unguarded speech when sober is chosen, not lapsed into.
list_adds: It makes careless speech one of three social intrusions (uninvited watching, untrusted visiting) that offend the whole town.

note: Kural 402 likens the unlearned man's desire to speak to a desire for womanhood in one without breasts; Pazhamozhi 16 likens his challenge to the learned to a lame man wanting to play with an elephant.
teaches: Both frame the unlearned man's ambition as desire without the faculty, but Pazhamozhi moves it from wanting to speak to picking a fight, where the lame man's wish also courts danger.
list_adds: its image adds danger to incapacity, since an elephant can crush the lame man who wants to play.

note: Both say learning held by one who fears the assembly is useless: the Kural likens it to a sword in a coward's hand, Thirikadugam to a mute man's dream.
teaches: The two images name different failures: the sword is a power left unused, the mute's dream an experience that cannot be told, so together they say fear of the assembly blocks both action and communication.
list_adds: It sets the timid scholar beside an incapable heir to wealth and a trapped fish, three goods held that cannot be brought out.

note: Acharakkovai 7 classes sexual union and eating as kinds of எச்சில்; Sivavakkiyar says the pure body itself came from எச்சில், and honey and milk are எச்சில் too.
teaches: The Siddhar takes the Acharakkovai's own classing of union as எச்சில் to its end: if union pollutes, every body and every food is born of pollution and the category cannot separate clean from unclean.

note: Kural 137 says conduct brings high standing and lapses bring blame; Pazhamozhi 15 uses the same ozhukkam and izhukkam pair as a proverb to judge speech among the unlearned.
teaches: The pairing shows the Kural's conduct couplet circulating as a proverb and being applied to a case the couplet never names, the choice of whom to speak before.
list_adds: it applies the conduct maxim to a particular act, eloquence in the wrong company, and so widens what counts as a lapse.

note: Naladiyar 254 says the unlearned man among the wise is a dog sitting if silent and a dog barking if he speaks; Pazhamozhi 13 says his unspoken insight is nothing.
teaches: Both refuse the unlearned any good way to be present among the learned, the Naladiyar by contempt for his person, Pazhamozhi by an argument that an unshown insight is no insight.
list_adds: it argues from the proverb on speech rather than from an insulting image, so the denial rests on how insight is shown, not on what the man is.

note: Acharakkovai 15 says one who scorns brahmins perishes; Kural 134 says a brahmin's birth itself is ruined when his conduct fails.
teaches: The Kural adds the condition the Acharakkovai leaves out: reverence owed to the brahmin by birth lapses with his conduct, so the two books disagree on whether birth alone commands it.
list_adds: It sets brahmins with the elements, the cow, the sun and the moon as cosmic things owed reverence, a rank the Kural makes conditional on conduct.

note: Verse 9 calls lust for women not one's own what fools love; verse 19 says the man at another's door by night hangs by a thread.
teaches: Within the book the same act is first a fool's desire and then a mortal danger, so the book judges it both by the wanting and by the result.

note: 60 likens Valavan to the strong ox that drags the salt cart's sunken wheel out of the rut on the road from the backwaters to the hill country; Akananuru 140 likens the speaker's suffering to that of the ox yoked to the father's salt cart sunk in deep mire.
teaches: The salt cart in the mire is a shared image of the coastal trade road, and the two books use opposite ends of it: the puram poet praises the king as the ox that frees the wheel, the akam speaker feels like the ox straining under it, so one working scene serves for strength in one and for heartache in the other.

note: Acharakkovai 5 bars one in எச்சில் from touching brahmins and other sacred things; Sivavakkiyar asks why water in the mouth is called எச்சில் while the Veda churned in the same mouth is not.
teaches: The Siddhar turns the category the Acharakkovai uses to protect the brahmin against the brahmin's own recitation, showing that the purity rule depends on exempting the sacred mouth from it.

note: Verse 4 has one rise worshipping father and mother; verse 16 names five elders, parents among them, to be worshipped as gods.
teaches: Verse 16 supplies the rank that verse 4's daily act presupposes, and shows the dawn rite honours only two of the five elders owed god-like worship.

note: 10 says the Chola, seeing a proven wrong, weighs it fairly and punishes fittingly (ஒப்ப நாடி அத்தக ஒறுத்தி); Kural 561 defines a king as one who inquires fittingly and punishes in proportion (தக்காங்கு நாடி ... ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது).
teaches: The two share the very words for inquiry and proportion, so the Kural's definition of the just king reads like a rule drawn out of praise such as this, and 10 adds what 561 leaves out: the sentence is softened for the one who comes and stands at the king's feet.

note: Kural 131 puts ஒழுக்கம் above life because it gives excellence; Acharakkovai 1 says what conduct grows from, naming eight inner virtues as its seed.
teaches: Read together, the Kural's command to guard conduct gets a source: the conduct to be guarded is not a set of rules but the outgrowth of gratitude, patience and the rest.
list_adds: It makes rule-bound conduct the fruit of eight ethical virtues, so a ritual code is founded on ethics before any ritual rule is given.

note: Naladiyar 255 has the worthy keep their learning unspoken, even when asked, where it will not be taken in; Pazhamozhi 14 gives the cost of speaking there.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives the practice, silence even when asked, and Pazhamozhi gives the reason, that good words among the unlearned turn bad.
list_adds: it names the outcome the worthy avoid, the reversal of good into bad, which the quatrain leaves implicit.

note: On the reading that புலை names the outcaste person, Acharakkovai 6 makes the sight of a birth-group polluting; Kural 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from deeds.
teaches: The conflict holds only if புலை is a person and செய்தொழில் means conduct, so the pairing shows how the caste force of each verse rests on one disputed word.
list_adds: It sets a birth-group beside a dog and the heavenly bodies as one class of barred sights, a ranking by birth the Kural's verse denies.

note: Kural 1066 says asking even water for a cow degrades the tongue; Acharakkovai 12 says the worthy do not beg sandals even when they lack them.
teaches: The Acharakkovai brings the Kural's limit case of begging down to one's own bodily need and sets it inside a list of purity rules, so not begging becomes part of bodily propriety.
list_adds: It places the refusal to beg beside rules against touching oil and others' cloth, treating begging as a kind of defilement.

note: Kural 450 ranks leaving the company of the good as ten times worse than many enemies; Thirikadugam counts leaving the company of the great as what fools love.
teaches: The couplet measures the harm of leaving good company; the verse says why people still do it: fools want it, so the harm is chosen.
list_adds: It sets leaving good company beside adulterous desire and base resolve, making all three expressions of a fool's preferences.
